When I joined the school play, I hoped to stand in the bright light and speak the final lines. Instead, the director asked me to work (1) ____ the curtain. I would move the paper trees while the other pupils acted.

For the first two practices, I felt disappointed. I thought nobody would notice my work. Then our tree fell during a scene. The actors had to stop, and the director asked us to begin again. I suddenly understood that the scene (2) ____ on the work behind the curtain too.

I started to practise moving the trees without making a sound. To keep them steady, I held each one with (3) ____ hands instead of trying to carry two at once. Mina, who managed the lights, showed me the marks on the floor. I waited for her quiet signal before moving anything.

On the night of the play, one tree caught on a chair. I wanted to pull hard, but I (4) ____. Pulling would tear the paper. I lifted the tree slightly and moved the chair away with my foot. The next scene began on time. Nobody in the audience knew what had nearly happened.

Afterwards, Mina said, “That was a good (5) ____.” She had seen the problem and my response. I was pleased that someone had noticed, but I no longer needed everyone to (6) ____ me. From my place at the side, I had watched our work become one story. I asked the director if I could do the same (7) ____ in the next play. This time, it was my own (8) ____.

completed_passage:
When I joined the school play, I hoped to stand in the bright light and speak the final lines. Instead, the director asked me to work behind the curtain. I would move the paper trees while the other pupils acted.

For the first two practices, I felt disappointed. I thought nobody would notice my work. Then our tree fell during a scene. The actors had to stop, and the director asked us to begin again. I suddenly understood that the scene depended on the work behind the curtain too.

I started to practise moving the trees without making a sound. To keep them steady, I held each one with both hands instead of trying to carry two at once. Mina, who managed the lights, showed me the marks on the floor. I waited for her quiet signal before moving anything.

On the night of the play, one tree caught on a chair. I wanted to pull hard, but I paused. Pulling would tear the paper. I lifted the tree slightly and moved the chair away with my foot. The next scene began on time. Nobody in the audience knew what had nearly happened.

Afterwards, Mina said, “That was a good decision.” She had seen the problem and my response. I was pleased that someone had noticed, but I no longer needed everyone to praise me. From my place at the side, I had watched our work become one story. I asked the director if I could do the same job in the next play. This time, it was my own choice.
